The study used a circular cylinder with a diameter-based Reynolds number of 100 as the bluff body.
Five pairs of windward-suction-leeward-blowing (WSLB) actuators were used to control the wake of the cylinder.
An array of 33 velocity sensors were placed 2D downstream of the cylinder to provide feedback signals to the controller.
The deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method, specifically the proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm, was used to train the control strategy.
For the stationary cylinder case, the DRL-trained control strategy was able to reduce the mean velocity deficit in the wake by 99.5% compared to the uncontrolled case.

The same control strategy learned for the stationary cylinder was effective in suppressing the vortex-induced vibration (VIV) of the cylinder and reducing the mean velocity deficit by 96.5% in the locked-in case and 95.9% in the unlocked-in case.
The DRL training for the VIV cylinder case used transfer learning, starting with the well-trained neural networks from the stationary cylinder case.
The WSLB actuation strategy learned by the DRL agent involved operating the ±40° actuators with the greatest strength and the 0° actuator with the smallest strength.
The control strategy was able to quickly (within about 1 oscillation cycle) reduce the hydrodynamic forces on the cylinder to values very close to zero.
The controlled wake showed that the strong vortex shedding was constrained in the near wake (x < 2D), and only very weak vorticities were observed further downstream.
The findings from this study can provide insights for the design and operation of underwater structures and robotics to achieve hydrodynamic stealth.
The in-house GPU-accelerated lattice Boltzmann solver used in the numerical simulations could manage the averaged computational time for each trial control case within 6 minutes.
The cost function J used in the DRL training consisted of two components: the velocity deficit and the actuation energy, with a small weighting coefficient (10^-4) applied to the actuation term.
The DRL training process showed a fast improvement in the first 500 episodes, and then gradually converged to a mature control strategy.
The learnt control strategy was able to balance the cylinder's hydrodynamic drag during cruising, making the wake nearly uniform.
